To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the discriminant functions of voxel‐based morphometries can be used to discriminate schizophrenia patients from controls with a sensitivity of 90.9% and specificity of 87.9% (area under the ROC curve = 0.94).
we found a set of brain regions whose combined volume was significantly different between schizophrenia patients and controls.

the combination of a number of brain measures, including the volume of the right amygdala, left hippocampus, left thalamus, and the left caudate nucleus, can be used to discriminate between schizophrenia patients and healthy subjects.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the relationship between brain structure and function in healthy subjects and in patients with neuropsychiatric disorders, with a special interest in the study of the brain in schizophrenia.
the study of the effects of the environment on the development of the brain, with a particular focus on the effects of stress, trauma and abuse.
the development of a new approach to the analysis and interpretation of neuroimaging data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a significant reduction of grey matter in the left hemisphere of the frontal lobe in schizophrenia patients compared to controls.
the brain abnormalities in schizophrenia are not limited to the frontal lobes, but involve other regions, such as the temporal lobes and the cerebellum.

the brain changes observed in schizophrenia are not limited to the medial temporal region but are distributed in a widespread manner, and that these changes are not specific to schizophrenia but are common to other psychiatric and neurologic disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the discriminant functions obtained using the whole brain data are able to discriminate between schizophrenia patients and healthy controls.
schizophrenia is characterized by a pattern of structural brain changes that are best described in terms of a loss of grey matter volume.
the discriminant functions derived from a combination of multiple structural brain measures can provide a more accurate diagnosis of schizophrenia than a single measure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple brain changes that can discriminate patients from healthy subjects and that the pattern of brain changes varies across the different groups.
the combination of several structural measures, rather than any one measure alone, is the most sensitive method to discriminate schizophrenia patients from controls.
a pattern of brain changes, rather than a single measure, is required to best distinguish schizophrenia patients from healthy controls.
